First describe the image: The attached figure is a truth table, with three columns respectively A, B, A  oxdot B. The operator values given in the four rows of the table are: when A=True, B=True, A  oxdot B=True; when A=True, B=False, A  oxdot B=True; when A=False, B=True, A  oxdot B=False; when A=False, B=False, A  oxdot B=True. Then reason: Test the expression 
eg(
eg A  oxdot B). Compute row by row: 1) A=True, B=True, then 
eg A=False, False  oxdot True=False, and the outer negation gives True. 2) A=True, B=False, then 
eg A=False, False  oxdot False=True, and the outer negation gives False. 3) A=False, B=True, then 
eg A=True, True  oxdot True=True, and the outer negation gives False. 4) A=False, B=False, then 
eg A=True, True  oxdot False=True, and the outer negation gives False. Therefore this expression is True only when A and B are both True, and is equivalent to A \land B.

method.method_draft:
First describe the image table and record the operator values. Test the expression \(
eg(
eg A  oxdot B)\) row by row: compute \(
eg A\), then apply the image-defined \( oxdot\) to inputs \((
eg A,B)\), then negate the result. The inner \(
eg A  oxdot B\) is true for all rows except when \(
eg A=False\) and \(B=True\), i.e. except when \(A=True,B=True\). Negating gives true exactly when both A and B are true, so the expression equals \(A\land B\).
